newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Scandal-hit U.N. Rwanda tribunal to resume trial.
newsitem.headline: Scandal-hit U.N. Rwanda tribunal to resume trial.

text.p: The scandal-hit U.N. Rwanda tribunal prepared to resume a genocide trial on Friday with new Secretary-General Kofi Annan promising "decisive action" to correct allegations of mismanagement and abuses.
A tribunal spokeswoman said the trial of a Hutu former government official, Jean-Paul Akayesu, charged with genocide and crimes against humanity, would resume on Friday because witnesses had arrived.

Akayesu's previously adjourned trial failed to start on Thursday because prosecution witnesses had not arrived from Rwanda. The justice ministry in Kigali blamed the tribunal, saying it had sought travel documents for the witnesses only 48 hours earlier.

Charges of mismanagement and unethical practices at the U.N. war crimes court took centre stage on Friday with Annan, in office for just a week, saying he was sending new personnel to clean up the court.
One of the tribunal's own judges joined the attacks on Friday.

"The atmosphere here is no good. It has been poisoned, there is no good cooperation between the staff and it is worse than in any other organisation that I have ever worked in," Lennart Aspegren of Sweden told reporters.

Annan on Thursday said through his spokesman he would take "decisive action" to make changes in the administrative apparatus of the tribunal, plagued by problems since it was set up in the north Tanzania town of Arusha.

"The moral weight of this body is enormous and those responsible for carrying out that work must meet the highest ethical and professional standards," he said, according to U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard.
Karl Paschke of Germany, the U.N. inspector general, has prepared a report on the alleged abuses in the tribunal, and Eckhard said Annan would take action once he had a chance to review it.
"But even before it is complete changes have and will be made in the administrative areas of the tribunal."
Eckhard said a new acting chief of administration, Mohammed Said of Ethiopia, had been sent to Arusha last month, replacing George Anderson of Liberia who had left in October.

In addition, Mario Cianci, who holds Italian and U.S. nationality, was going to Arusha soon to temporarily take over personnel. That position is held by Andronico Adede of Kenya, a legal officer who previously worked in New York.

The Arusha controversy is fraught with racial overtones, with European employees complaining that the tribunal's administrators have given jobs to relatives and friends who have no qualifications and discriminated against non-Africans.
But Adede on Friday offered a defence of his record to reporters after the U.N. report put him at the centre of allegations of mismanagement and unethical behaviour.

"I think that there is close to a deliberate attempt to pin failure on me. But what do they do with the fact that seven people are in custody, four more are coming and this fulfils the mandate of the tribunal," Adede said.

Twenty-one people have been indicted by the tribunal including Akayesu. Eight suspects are still at large, seven are held in Arusha including Akayesu, four are in detention in Cameroon and the United States and Switzerland hold one each.
Adede complained that when he arrived in Arusha in November 1995 he was forced to start from scratch without assistance, and office or proper communications facilities.
Arusha was chosen as the seat of the tribunal despite its primitive telecommunications and poor transport links.

But tribunal judges separately complained that they had encountered problems with Adede's registry. They spoke to reporters on Friday about problems of mismanagement, abuses of recruitment and funds and a complete lack of cooperation from the registry.
